21                                        Abstract

22   Anaerobic digestion (AD) is a promising technology to recover bioenergy from biodegradable

23   biomass, including cellulosic wastes. Through a few fractionation/separation techniques,

24    cellulose has demonstrated its potential in AD, but the performance of the process is rather

25    substrate-specific as cellulolysis bacteria are sensitive to the enzyme-substrate interactions.

26   Cellulosome is a self-assembled enzyme complex with many functionalized modules in the

27    bacteria, which has been gradually studied, however the genomic fingerprints of the culture-

28    specific cellulosome in AD are relatively unclear especially under processing conditions. To

29    clarify the key factors affecting the cellulosome induced cellulolysis, this review summarized

30    the most recent publications of AD regarding the fates of cellulose, sources and functional

31   genes of cellulosome, and omics methods for functional analyses. Different processes for

32    organic treatment including applying food grinds in sewer, biomass valorization, cellulose

33    fractionation,  micro-aeration,  and  enzymatic  hydrolysis  enhanced  fermentation,  were

34    highlighted to support the sustainable development of AD technology.

35

36   Keyword: Anaerobic digestion, cellulolysis, biomass, cellulosome, cellulosome-embedded

37    prokaryotes

55   1. Cellulosic Substrates in AD

56       Climate change has started to demonstrate its dramatic impacts on human society and

57    global environment. Anaerobic digestion (AD) among the biochemical conversion practices to

58   reduce greenhouse gases emissions (e.g., non-point sources CH4) has become a critical trend

59   toward decarbonized economy (Meckling et al., 2017). AD is a widely used technology for

60   waste management, energy recovery, and biorefinery for various organic wastes and biomass.

61    Lignocellulose has significant potential for the production of biogas and biochemicals due to

62     its high energy value building block components in the substrate, e.g., cellulose. Cellulose is

63   an abundant and valuable resources in food waste (FW); agriculture waste (AW); and primary

64   sludge (PS) from the municipal wastewater treatment system (Li et al., 2021; Zhuang et al.,

65   2020). The predicted global production of FW will reach 2.5 billion tons in fresh weight by

66   2025 (Liu et al., 2020), of which its compositions differ significantly among regions and

67    sources (e.g., family, catering, and food industry) (Wang et al., 2020a), and carbohydrates

68    contributed from cereal, staple food, and lignocellulose account for approximately 35.5-69.0%

69    of FW by weight (Zou et al., 2020). AW is the largest source of cellulosic biomass, of which

70     its annual production is over 3 billion tons in fresh weight; the global AW is expected to

71    increase by 60% higher than the current value by 2050 (Tripathi et al., 2019). Finally, cellulose

72    in municipal wastewater accounts for 25-30% of total solids before being treated in the sewage

73    treatment works (Ahmed et al., 2019). The cellulosic biomass contributed considerably to the

74    total organic loads, and can increase energy consumption (through aeration) of the overall

75   system if not separated (as PS) from the influent (Ahmed et al., 2019).

76      With the  potential  to produce  easily digestible glucose,  cellulose-rich  solids have

77   demonstrated its value in AD (Crutchik et al., 2018). However, the hydrolysis rate of cellulose

78   has often become the rate limiting factor of the AD. The fundamental genomic approach to

79    investigate the impacts is also limited. Based on the recent publications, this paper aims to



                                          4

80   provide an overview of the publication within the past five years to expend the technical and

 81   economic feasibilities of AD. While the substrate-related factors regarding to this approach

 82   have been reviewed elsewhere (Wang et al., 2019), this study will focus more on the bio-related

 83    factors such as cellulose and cellulosome characterization; cellulose degrading microbes/genes;

 84   genomic foundation of cellulose hydrolysis; and genomic driven AD applications toward more

 85    effective and efficient operation.

 87   2. Hydrolysis of Lignocellulosic Biomass in AD


 88    2.1 Characteristics lignocellulosic biomass and their hydrolysis in AD

 89      The average biogas production of different lignocellulosic and cellulosic substrates with

 90    different chemical compositions, treatment processes, and biogas productivities have been

 91   demonstrated in Table 1. Although due to the high quantity in the substrate the hydrolysis of

 92    the cellulosic component has served as the main concern of the AD, the rates of cellulolysis

 93   can be severely interfered by the other building block components in the plant cell wall micro-

 94    structure. Lignocellulosic biomass is composed of cellulose, hemicellulose, lignin, and small

 95   amounts of other compounds (such as protein and pectin). Pabón-Pereira et al. (2020; 2012)

 96    indicated that cellulosic biomass demonstrated quite different methanogenesis potential, i.e.,

 97   0.14 to 0.37 L CH4∙g VS-1 under biochemical methane potential (BMP) tests. The conceptual

 98    structure of the plant cell wall, with the spatial arrangement and related hydrolyzing enzyme

 99    for each building block chemicals has been demonstrated in Figure 3 and 4.

100        Cellulose is the key component of plant cell walls, which exists in fiber forms embedded

101    in a complex matrix of other building block chemicals . The cellulosic long-chain is composed

102    of hundreds to thousands ᴅ-glucopyranose units connected with β-1,4-glycosidic linkages . The

103    micro-fibers are attached in line through hydrogen bonds, and the various forms and quantities

104    of the bonding resulted in the unique crystalline and amorphous domains of the biopolymer



                                           5

105   (Pensupa et al., 2017). As the arrangement patterns of the cellulose differ significantly from

106    the species and parts of the plants, different crystallinity, hydrophilicity, and accessibility of

107   enzyme to cellulose (Liu et al., 2016) are formed and resulted in different biodegradabilities in

108    the AD. Popovic et al. (2019) reported that the hydrolysis of amorphous cellulose to aqueous

109   glucose has negative change in Gibbs free energy (at 0 to 100°C), indicating that the reaction

110     is thermodynamically favorable, i.e., the chemical reaction could happen without extra energy

111    input. However, the change in Gibbs free energy from crystal cellulose to aqueous glucose

112   could vary from -6.6 to 3.0 kJ/mol depending on the types of crystal forms and reaction

113    temperature, suggesting increased difficulties in hydrolysis of crystalline cellulose. Although

114    the reaction is thermodynamic favorable (Gibbs free energy is negative) the reaction rate was

115     still affected by the physical structure of the substrate and the catalyst factor in the system.

116   During hydrolysis, the crystal cellulose is peeled off layer by layer, and can be accelerated by

117   changing the ultrastructure from cellulose I to cellulose II or cellulose III (Horikawa et al.,

118   2013; Wada et al., 2010).

119       Hemicelluloses are polysaccharides attached amorphously with the cellulosic fibers. Xylan

120    (a five carbon, C5 sugar) and mannan (a C6 sugar) are the most abundant hemicellulose in

121   hardwood/herbal and softwood, respectively. Different enzyme systems are responsible to the

122    digestion of hemicelluloses and cellulose. Previous BMP tests showed that the hydrolysis rate

123    of hemicellulose was faster than that of cellulose and pure cellulose showed higher methane

124    potential than hemicellulose (Li et al., 2018a). Thermodynamically, hemicellulose hydrolysis

125     is an endotherm and hence extra energy or additional product is needed in the reaction (Tizazu

126  & Moholkar, 2018). Some hemicellulose could also inhibit cellulolysis (Chen et al., 2020).

127   However, pentose and hexose are important carbon and energy sources to be completely

128    utilized in an AD (Chen et al., 2019).





                                           6

129       Lignin is a three-dimensional biopolymer composed of three monolignols (Islam et al.,

130   2020). It fills up the space among the cellulose, hemicellulose, and pectin, and forms into a

131    crosslinked network structure with various types of linkages, i.e., covalent, hydrogen bonds,

132   and van der Waals forces (Speight, 2020). The massive aromatic nucleus in lignin matrix makes

133     it extremely recalcitrant against chemical and biological degradation (Khan & Ahring, 2021).

134   The hydrolysis of lignocellulosic structure is related to many substrate-related interactions

135   between  enzymes  and  lignin.  The  biodegradability  of  lignocellulosic  biomass  in

136   methanogenesis AD could vary from 0.1% to 76.4%, and the lag phase could range from 0 to

137   27.4 days (Li et al., 2018a; Ma et al., 2019). Lignin may absorb and/or deactivate the enzymes

138    (Li et al., 2018b). Complete decomposition of lignin is a slow process that could last for

139    centuries (Zabel & Morrell, 2020). Lignin depolymerization in AD are mainly carried out by

140   Spirochaeta and Chitinophaga (Pandit et al., 2016). The biodegradation process starts from

141   breakages of side chains, functional groups, and/or aromatic nucleus, and complete degradation

142    of lignin (breakage of the aromatic rings) have never been observed anaerobically. With limited

143   energy yield lignin depolymerization often couples with the metabolisms of easily degradable

144    substrates. Some  studies  found  that  sulfate  reducing  bacteria  of  Desulfomicrobium,

145   Desulfomicrobium, and Desulfobulbus genus could decompose lignin by using sulfate as

146    election acceptor (Wang et al., 2013; Yamashita et al., 2011).

147

148    2.2 Enzymatic system for cellulolysis and glycoside hydrolase families

149       Cellulose degradation in bioconversion process has been mainly carried out by cellulase

150   produced from anaerobic or aerobic microorganisms, such as bacteria and fungi. Cellulases

151    include a few types of enzymes which can be divided into three categories according to the

152    catalytic functions,  i.e., exoglucanases (1,4-D-glucan glucanohydrolases and 1,4-Dglucan

153    cellobiohydrolases), endoglucanases (1,4-D-glucan-4-glucanohydrolases), and β-glucosidases



                                           7

154    (β-glucoside glucohydrolases) (Bhati & Sharma, 2020; Lynd et al., 2002; Schwarz, 2001).

155   Complete hydrolysis of cellulose relies on the synergetic reactions of the enzymes,  i.e.,

156   exoglucanases hydrolyze the crystalline cellulose from either the reducing end or non-reducing

157   end of the cellulosic chain (Teeri, 1997; Zhang et al., 2018); endoglucanases randomly break

158    the glycosidic linkages in the amorphous  cellulose, releasing large numbers of short-chain

159    cellulose and available free ends for exoglucanases (Brunecky et al., 2017); and β-glucosidases

160   break the glycosidic linkages of di-glucosides, alkyl/aryl glucosides, cyanogenic glucosides,

161   and oligoglucosides for glucose (Thapa et al., 2020). In this process, the main rate-limiting step

162     is  the  hydrolysis  of  crystalline  cellulose  (by  exoglucanases),  while  the number  of

163   exoglucanases in most AD system is too low to support the cellulolysis at high efficiency.

164       In addition to cellulases, hemicellulases also participate in lignocellulose hydrolysis. The

165    related enzymes can be divided into three major types according to the target positions of

166   enzymes on hemicellulose chains. Exohemicellulases, such as β-D-xylosidase and β-D-

167   mannosidase, can break the glycosidic bonds at free ends of the hemicellulose chains;

168    endohemicellulases, such as β-D-xylanase, β-D-mannanase, can break glycosidic bonds at

169   random positions or specific positions; and additional enzymes such as acetyl xylan esterase

170    are required to remove side-chain hemicellulose (Franco et al., 2004; Razeq et al., 2018).

171       Since both of cellulases and hemicellulases are both responsible catalyzing lignocellulose

172    hydrolysis and share some common features, the enzymes were grouped into Carbohydrate-

173   Active Enzymes (CAZymes) database with some other enzymes with hydrolytic activities for

174   carbohydrates such as starch and chitin. They have been further classified into 169 glycosyl

175    hydrolases (GHs) and 18 carbohydrate esterases (CEs) families (Lombard et al., 2014) based

176   on the nucleic acid or amino acid sequence enzymes’ catalytic modules. Some GHs are

177    multifunctional, having high catalytic activity to several kinds of cellulosic substrates. For

178   example,  the endoglucanase EG5C-1 from  Bacillus  subtilis BS-5 can hydrolyze both



                                           8

179   carboxymethyl cellulose (CMC) and p-nitrophenyl-β-D-cellobioside at hydrolytic activities of

180   4,170 and 2,550 U/μmol, respectively (Zhan et al., 2018). CbXyn10C and Bgxg1 expressed

181   from Lactobacillus plantarum also showed hydrolytic activities on xylan, avicel, and CMC

182   (Guo et al., 2019). A total of 39 cellulases and hemicellulases can be related to Proteiniphilum

183   saccharofermentans M3/6 for the degradation of arabinan, xylan, mannan, and β-glucans

184   (Tomazetto et al., 2018). The example illustrates the complexity of cellulolysis enzyme system

185    in AD, and the necessity of genomic-based study for understanding such system in the microbes.

186

187    2.3 Cellulosomal enzymatic components in AD

188    AD is an engineered environment with limited electron acceptors, in which the microbes

189   cannot completely oxidize the organic matters for energy. To survive in the critical condition,

190   cellulosomes was evolved in anaerobes for effective uptake of the hydrolysate after cellulolysis.

191   Cellulosome is a function-specific unit composed of catalytic proteins and non-catalytic

192    proteins (Wang et al., 2019). Cellulosomes have been identified on the surface of several

193    anaerobes, i.e., most of which are bacteria and some fungi. In different species, cellulosomes

194    present with specific molecular arrangement with varying degrees of complexity (Artzi et al.,

195   2017). An example of cellulosomes formed by Clostridium clariflavum and their assembly

196    structure proposed by Artzi et al. (2015) has been illustrated in Figure 4. The non-catalytic

197    proteins are referred to scaffoldins (Ding & Bayer, 2020; Ichikawa et al., 2014), which are

198    large proteins serving as foundation of the cellulosomal complex. The functional domains on

199    scaffoldins are carbohydrate-binding modules (CBMs) and cohesions (Leis et al., 2017), of

200   which CBMs are the protein domains that can tightly bind to the lignocellulose fibers, and

201   cohesions contains GHs and CEs as major catalytic proteins for hydrolysis. The scaffoldins

202   can contain up to hundreds of cohesions regions for various specific types of substrates and

203    thus the fixed catalytic subunits can continuously conduct hydrolysis.



                                           9

204       Cellulosomes can consist of more than one scaffoldins binding to each other by cohesin-

205    dockerin. For example, the cellulosome formed by Clostridium thermocellum can have at least

206   8 types of scaffoldins (Hong et al., 2014). ScaA is the scaffoldin with CBM, it has type I cohesin

207   and type II dockerin (Figure 4) (Bule et al., 2017). It can anchor on the cell surface by

208   connecting to ScaF or ScaD with type II dockerin-cohesin connection (Bule et al., 2018). ScaE

209     is the cell-free scaffoldin, which can create a large cell-free cellulosome by connecting its type

210     II cohesins with type II dockerins of ScaH/L and ScaA. In addition, free uncomplexed enzymes

211   and  cell-bound  cellulosome complexes were produced  simultaneously. The  structure,

212   compositions and corresponding substrates of cellulosomes are regulated and varied by the

213    nature of the growth substrates and the host microbes. Artzi et al. (2015) demonstrated that the

214   cellulosome proteins produced from Clostridium clariflavum were regulated by the type of

215    substrates including cellobiose, microcrystalline cellulose, and acid-pretreated switchgrass.

216   The outer membrane receptor protein and sensor may have potential function of carbohydrate-

217    sensing and CAZyme gene regulation (Kougias et al., 2018). A bioinformatics study for

218    screening the cellulosomal modules found that beyond the cellulolysis, 23.6% of the dockerin-

219    containing proteins were related to alternative biological processes such as protein degradation

220    or putative lysozyme activity in the bovine rumen microbiome (Bensoussan et al., 2017). The

221   dockerin-cohesin systems in a wide variety of different biological and cellular processes

222   implied its possible evolutionary directions and potential application for cellulosomes complex.

223   The  multi-enzymatic  systems  could  serve  as  a  powerful  tool  that  assists  in  novel

224    biotechnologies.

225       In summary, cellulosomes can improve the synergistic efficiency among hydrolytic

226    subunits; prevent a single low-efficiency enzyme from adsorbing cellulose and competition

227   between different enzymes due to the same absorption site; and have a continuous cellulolysis





                                           10

228   on long-chain lignocellulose. Its modular nature makes it highly efficient in cellulolysis and

229    feasible to be artificially manufactured through biotechnology for large-scale applications.

231   3. Genetic Fingerprint of Cellulolysis


232    3.1 Cellulolysis and methanogenesis of anaerobic microbes

233       Hydrolytic microbes  are key  participants  of AD. The most predominant  bacterial

234    hydrolyzers belong to several phyla,  i.e., Firmicutes, Bacteroidetes, Proteobacteria, and

235    Chloroflexi. The abundances of those hydrolytic bacteria are related to the process conditions

236   such as organic loading, solids retention time (SRT), temperature, and types of substrates (Chen

237    et  al., 2016; Nguyen et  al., 2019b). Meanwhile,  it is difficult to estimate the taxonomic

238    borderline of hydrolyzers, acidogens and acetogens. For example, more than hydrolysis of

239    cellulose, some hydrolyzers such as Clostridium cellulolyticum can further oxidize the glucose

240   and produce acetate H2 and CO2  (Jia et  al., 2018). To understand the niche of those

241    multifunction players may help to design the system with better robustness and stability.

242       Anaerobic hydrolytic fungi belong to phylum Neocallimastigomycota. Compared to the

243    hydrolytic bacteria, hydrolytic fungi have rhizoid system which provides ability of mechanical

244    disruption of the lignocellulose tissues through invasive growth (Dollhofer et  al., 2015).

245   Neocallimastigomycota are also the only fungi forming cellulosomes, of which the genes

246   encoding cellulosomal enzyme may be obtained from hydrolytic bacteria through horizontal

247   gene transfer (Murphy et al., 2019). Although with some imperfection such as low abundance

248    in system and easy to be wash out, anaerobic fungi have great potential in engineering

249    application. Fungal bioaugmentation for enhancing cellulolysis in AD increased the methane

250    yield by 15-33% for treating cereal crops/straws and cow manure (Akyol et al., 2019). Using

251   immobilized fungi in AD increased the methane yields of batch and continuous flow system

252   by 50% (from around 250 ml/g VSS increased to around 375 ml/g VSS) and 13-31% (from



                                           11

253   around 600 (Day 0 to Day 10) and 4,200 ml/d (Day 70 to Day 90) increased to around 680 and

254   5300 ml/d, respectively), respectively (Guo et al., 2021).

255

256    3.2 Genome-wide analysis of cellulosome system and cellulosomics

257      Fundamental cellulosome study has been conducted after a comprehensive and time-

258   consuming procedure. The most accurate way to study the enzyme system is by cultivating

259    specific microbes for pure enzyme analysis. However, only a small fraction of anaerobic

260    bacteria can be grown in the laboratory. The current understanding of cellulosomes were

261    thereafter limited only within a finite number of bacteria strains. With the rapid development

262    of novel sequencing technology, nevertheless, new perspectives for deciphering the complex

263   and ingenious cellulolysis system are constructed. The gene-centric cellulosome systematic

264   study approach can now screen and discover unknown CAZymes, dockerin-cohesin systems,

265    signal/regulation system, and other cellulosome-relative active substance (Smith et al., 2017).

266   Metagenome, whole-genome, and transcriptome sequencing approaches have been widely

267   used to investigate the cellulolytic microbes and cellulosome relative proteins.

268      Metagenomics and transcriptomics study provide powerful tools in cellulolysis research.

269  AD is a mix-culture microbial system and metagenome information can provide immediate

270    insights  of  the  major  participants  and  the  potential  metabolism  pathway  of  those

271   microorganisms. Transcriptomics analysis focuses on mRNA analysis of microbes, which is

272   an index of gene expression (Chen et al., 2017). It is the tool to compare different gene

273    expressions among distinct cell populations, or the gene expressions of a cell population

274   response to different environmental conditions. It is also a useful method to identify the

275   metabolism pathways, the cell signaling system, and the gene regulation models in biological

276    systems. For cellulosome study, transcriptomics has been applied to observe the changes in

277   gene expression of an engineered C. thermocellum strain as a response to change carbon



                                           12

278    sources from xylose to cellobiose (Tafur Rangel et al., 2020). Kougias et al. (2018) conducted

279   a shotgun metagenomics analysis on the AD treating pig manure and meadow grass. A total

280    of 151 genomes were recovered by binning process, while 80 of which were completely new

281   and   cannot   be   found    in    existing    database.   Uncultured   members    of

282    Bacteroidetes and Firmicutes were  indicated  to  play important  roles  for polysaccharide

283    degradation, among which the Firmicutes species, the number and functional roles of CBMs

284    of cellulosomes were different. Wilkens et al. (2017) identified 19,335 CAZymes genes from

285    four full-scale mesophilic AD treating sludge in municipal wastewater treatment plants by

286   metagenomic sequencing, A total of 10,374 genes belonged to 133 GH families and 2,064

287   belonged to 17 CE families. However, only 54% of the CAZymes genes were annotated with

288     its function and the others can only be classified into one enzyme family. The results indicated

289    that our knowledge of the CAZy subfamilies are limited, while more comprehensive database

290    is to be developed especially for the AD treating lignocellulosic biomass.

291        Potential  RsgI-like carbohydrate sensing  proteins were  identified with a group of

292    upregulated xylose hydrolytic enzymes. In addition, the candidate ABC transporters for xylose

293    transport and assimilation were also revealed in this transcriptomics study. By transcriptomic

294    analysis, Raman et al. (2011) observed in later stages of cellulose fermentation with C.

295   thermocellum ATCC 27405 that several cellulosomal catalytic subunits (i.e., mannanases,

296    xyloglucanase, pectate lyase, etc., belongs to GH families ) were significant upregulated for

297   degrading non-cellulolytic substrates. Increasing expression of non-cellulolytic enzymes in the

298    free cellulosomes during the latter stage of growing might be applicable for exposing the

299    cellulose from untapped resources. The protease inhibiting components were also expressed

300    progressively, which might protect the cellulosome from protease driven degradation.

301      At present, the sequencing technologies have been updated rapidly. The third-generation

302   sequencing platforms such as PacBio Sequel and Oxford Nanopore are able to generate more



                                           13

303    accurate sequence reads with enhanced information like DNA methylation signals. The

304    decreasing sequencing  costs would  also  allow  researchers  to pay more  attention on

305    cellulosomics. The extension of the genetic information database coupling with more analytical

306    tools will definitely help to understand and utilize the cellulosome system in AD.

307

308   4. Adjustment of Reaction Kinetics in Considering Cellulolysis


309    4.1 Micro-aeration for enhancing biodegradability of lignocellulosic biomass in AD

310       Microaerobic digestion has gained increased attention in recent years. This process refers

311    to the addition of a small well-controlled amount of air or oxygen into the AD. Although

312   oxygen has long been considered as an inhibitor to obligate anaerobes, many studies have

313   demonstrated improved  digestibility and  stability of AD processes under microaerobic

314    conditions (Botheju & Bakke, 2011; Nguyen & Khanal, 2018). The merits of this operational

315   approach include improved methane production, enhanced enzymatic hydrolysis, release of

316  VFA  accumulation, and  mitigation  of hydrogen  sulfide, which  facilitate  the  overall

317   performances of the AD systems (Charles et al., 2009; Fdz-Polanco et al., 2009; Johansen &

318   Bakke, 2006; Lim & Wang, 2013; Nguyen et al., 2019a). Specifically, an oxidation-reduction

319    potential (ORP)-based oxygenation approach, where ORP level varies linearly with the

320    logarithmic dissolved oxygen (DO) concentration, allows for a more precise control of

321    oxygen/air injection far below 0.1 mg/L into a digester (Khanal & Huang, 2003). Given these

322    advantages, several research groups have applied such microaerobic strategies for digestion of

323    lignocellulosic biomass such as corn/wheat/rice straw, napier grass, cow manure, etc. (Fu et al.,

324   2016a; Fu et al., 2016b; Nguyen et al., 2019a; Tsapekos et al., 2017; Wang et al., 2020c). Fu

325    et al. (2016a; 2016b) reported simultaneous improvements in methane yield and VS removal

326    efficiency in batch thermophilic digestions of corn straw either by air pretreatment or by direct

327    air injection. While pretreatment obtained 16.24% higher in methane production, direct



                                           14

328    treatment achieved 28.45% higher in methane production and 29.43% higher in VS removal,

329    respectively. Nguyen et al. (2019a) developed an ORP-based intermittent microaerobic AD

330   system to treat napier grass and achieved a stable methane yield of 80.8±9.6 N CH4 mL/VS g

331   when picomolar oxygen was applied by setting the ORP + 25 mV above the strict anaerobic

332    baseline every other day.

333      The underlying microbial mechanism is that the supply of insufficient oxygen creates a

334   unique ecological niche suitable for both anaerobes and aerobes, promoting a new balance

335   between hydrolytic bacteria, fermentative bacteria, methanogens, as well as facultative bacteria

336   (Nguyen & Khanal, 2018; Nguyen et al., 2019a; Wu et al., 2021). The facultative oxygen

337   scavenger may rapidly consume the dissolved oxygen in system, shielding the surrounding

338   anaerobic  cells from  direct oxygen  attack.  Moreover,  facultative  anaerobes  perform

339   thermodynamic  advantages  over  strictly  anaerobes,  making  them  grow  faster  and

340   predominance under microaerobic conditions (Nguyen et al., 2019a; Rittmann & McCarty,

341   2001). Wu et al. (2021) unveiled the metabolic pathway of an ORP-based microaerobic

342    digestion of lignocellulose by genome-centric metagenomics. It confirmed that the cellulolytic

343    facultative Proteiniphilum  strains repeatedly dominated  in microaerobic system, which

344   encoded rich extracellular enzymes in lignocellulose hydrolysis, fermentative pathway to

345    formate, acetate or propionate, as well as complete aerobic respiration pathway to CO2.

346   Meanwhile,  the  high  oxygen  affinity  bd-type  terminal  oxidases  among  oxidative

347   phosphorylation pathway in Proteiniphilum strains were assumed to closely associated with

348   such picomolar oxygen conditions. Moreover, many microbial community analyses also

349    reported that microaeration led to higher abundance and activity of hydrolytic bacteria,

350    especially the phylum Firmicutes (Fu et al., 2016a; Lim et al., 2014). In addition, the strictly

351   anaerobes (especially the methanogens), as well as facultative bacteria, both have been widely

352   found to possess various antioxidant enzymes (e.g., superoxide dismutase (SOD), superoxide



                                           15

353    reductase (SOR), etc.), overcoming the oxidative stress under microaerobic circumstances

354    (Imlay, 2002). Microaeration triggers a synergistic relationship between hydrolytic facultative

355    heterotrophs and anaerobic methanogens, which  facilitate the energetic conversion from

356    intermediates to methane in order to maintain an overall stability of AD processes (shown in

357   Figure 4, by Nguyen et al. (2019a) and Wu et al. (2021)).

358       In application, microaeration significantly relies on the appropriate oxygen injection into

359    the digester, which refers to aeration type  (air or pure oxygen), method (direct  inject,

360    electrolytic  aeration,  etc.),  frequency (one  time,  intermittently,  or  continuously), and

361    application stage (pre-, post-, or simultaneous treatment) (Girotto et al., 2018; González-

362   González & Cuadros, 2015; Rafieenia et al., 2017). While excess aeration resulted in an

363   overwhelming deterioration to AD process (Xu et al., 2014), inadequate aeration also requires

364   a new microbial balance in system, which influence the system stability (Zhu et al., 2009).

365   Thus, for widely use of microaerobic approach in cellulose digestion, fully understanding of

366    cellulose conversion pathway under different microaeration control process are necessary.

367      The biological process control and oxygen uptake is a crucial parameter for metabolic

368   pathway and system optimization. The oxygen transfer efficiency (OTE) decreases during the

369    aeration process because of changing sludge conditions can be quantified by the α-factor, the

370    ratio of OTE in the process condition to that in clean water (Metcalf et al., 2014). When

371    microaeration  is performed as a pretreatment method, the α-factor should be carefully

372   monitored because the excess DO could reduce the methane potential, and insufficient oxygen

373   could potentially fail to produce the beneficial effect of microaeration  (Girotto et al., 2018).

374   The intensity of microaeration measured in terms of aeration or oxygen flow rate is the key

375    control parameter determining the effects of microaeration (Nguyen & Khanal, 2018). In the

376    microaeration system, high mixed liquor suspended solids (MLSS) could systematically





                                           16

377    decrease the α-factor, and ultra-fine bubble diffusers could suffer from greater oxygen transfer

378    depression (i.e., fouling, viscosity, and bubble coalescence) (Garrido-Baserba et al., 2017).

380    4.2 Pretreatment to improve biodegradability of lignocellulosic biomass before AD

381        Integrating pretreatment techniques with AD to improve the hydrolysis efficiency has

382    attracted significant attentions for the valorization of lignocellulosic biomass (Xu et al., 2019).

383    In biorefinery, pretreatment process has been developed mainly to decompose, migrate, and

384   modify the building block chemicals to facilitate the enzyme-substrate interactions (Liu et al.,

385   2016). The key mechanisms  applied  in  pretreatment  process design  include biomass

386   depolymerization (Li et al., 2020), reduction and form-shifting of the crystalline cellulose in

387    the substrate(Ling et al., 2020), breakage of the lignin obstruction (Sabeeh et al., 2020),

388   removal of inhibitors (Koupaie et al., 2019), creation of more accessible binding sites for

389    hydrolytic enzymes (Kainthola et al., 2019a), and ease the growth of methanogens (Zhen et al.,

390    2017). Pretreatment is a substrate- and product-specific unit operation, for which significant

391   amount of energy, chemicals, and/or other resources (e.g., space) are invested for waste

392    valorization (Zhang et al., 2020). Based on the decomposition principles and process conditions,

393    the modern pretreatment can be classified into three categories, i.e., physical, chemical, and

394    biological processes, which summarized in Table 2 and discussed in the following sections.

395       Physical pretreatment aims at increasing the surface area and biomass porosity to increase

396    the accessibility of enzyme (Leu & Zhu, 2013) and/or anaerobic microorganism (when

397   cellulosome is of concern) to the substrate surface (Wang et al., 2019). It can also reduce the

398    viscosity of the slurry substrate for better agitation even under high solid loads (Lu et al., 2020).

399   The techniques involve in physical pretreatment include mechanical, thermal, ultrasonic, and

400   microwave process (Wang et  al., 2020b). The mechanical pretreatment such as milling,

401    grinding, and drum rotating are developed to reduce the particle size of substrates and/or



                                           17

402   improve the mixing between the treated solids and liquid (Carrere et al., 2016). Kang et al.

403   (2019) reported an increased biodegradability index by 13.5% when the size of hybrid

404   Pennisetum biomass decreased from 0.83 mm to 0.25 mm. When the size of wheat straw

405   reduced from 50 mm to 2 mm, the methane yield increased from 285 to 334 mL/g VS (Menardo

406    et al., 2012). The methane yield also increased 53% when the particle size of Laminariaceae

407    spp. Biomass was reduced to 76-836 μm (Tedesco et al., 2014). However, previous studies also

408    indicated that, in some occasions, further reduction substrate particle size could result in over

409   production of VFAs which inhibited the biogas production (Izumi et al., 2010). Thermal

410    pretreatment is typically carried out by pressurized vessel, in which the substrate can be swelled

411   under pressure and heat (Banu & Kavitha, 2017; Zhou et al., 2015). Depends on the process

412    condition, thermal pretreatment may induce different chemical reactions such as hemicellulose

413    hydrolysis, hydrogen bonds breakage in crystalline celluloses, and/or changes in lignin phase

414   (Veluchamy & Kalamdhad, 2017). Hydrothermal pretreatment coupled with AD was proven

415    to complete removal of hemicellulose, for which the cellulose-enriched biomass can be used

416    for biomethane production (Kaur et al., 2019). Biomass treated under mild and eco-friendly

417   hydrothermal condition reduced the formation of inhibitors prior to AD (Dasgupta & Chandel,

418   2019). Passos et al. (2018) reported a 96% increase of methane yield when coffee husk and

419   microalgae were pretreated at 120°C for 60 min. The methane yield was increased by 57.7%

420   (344 mL/ g VS) when the wheat straw was pretreated at 180°C for 1 h (Rajput & Visvanathan,

421   2018). Microwave treatment is another type of thermal pretreatment of which electromagnetic

422    radiation was applied for substrate decomposition at a wide range of frequency and wavelength

423   (Marin et al., 2010). This pretreatment process can effectively increase the methane yield of

424  AD (Wang et al., 2021), while some negative impacts were reported when it was applied on

425   low lignin or lignocellulose substrate such as food or vegetable/fruit wastes (Atelge et al., 2020).

426    Ultrasonic pretreatment mechanically disrupts the fiber, cell structure and floc matrix through



                                           18

427    the shear force by the vibration probe (Elliott & Mahmood, 2007). Pilli et al. (2016) applied

428    ultrasonic pretreatment (750 w, 20 kHz) on PS and reported an increase of 17.3% higher

429   methane yield (273 mL/g VS) than the control study. Ormaechea et al. (2018) found that

430    ultrasonic pretreated cattle manure reached to 460 mL/g VS, which was 58.6% higher than the

431    control. Microwave and ultrasonic pretreatment are effective but both require high energy and

432   maintenance fee when large scale application is of concern (Hassan et al., 2018).

433      Chemical  pretreatment  is  a common  approach  to  reduce biomass  recalcitrant  of

434    lignocellulosic biomass in biorefinery (Islam et al., 2020). Acids, alkaline and oxidants have

435   been applied under various conditions to destroy or fractionate the complex structure and to

436   improve biodegradability of the substrate (Nguyen et al., 2021). Alkaline pretreatment is a

437   widely applied strategy for low recalcitrant biomass which can be conducted at ambient room

438   temperature and pressure with modest energy consumption and without producing harmful by-

439   product for downstream process (Behera et al., 2014; Shah, 2018). Alkaline also has the

440    function  of  swelling, and  solubilization  of COD and  other macromolecules, such  as

441   carbohydrates and protein to increase the digestibility of substrate (Nguyen et al., 2021). You

442    et al. (2019) reported an increase of 38.5% methane yield when conducting the co-digestion of

443  NaOH and CaO pretreated corn stover and swine manure. Zhu et al. (2020) tested the AD

444   performance of wheat straw by using 2.0% alkaline liquor and 1:3 synthetic urine, they

445   obtained increase in the methane yield by 68% and 56%, respectively. Acid pretreatment is

446    another effective method to break down the lignocellulosic structure (van der Waals force,

447   hydrogen bonds and covalent bonds) and for higher AD performance (Mussoline et al., 2013;

448   Wada et al., 2010). Dilute acid (DA) pretreatment assists the higher reaction rates of AD and

449   improves the susceptibility of cellulose to hydrolysis (Amin et al., 2017). In a study conducted

450   by Song et al. (2014), the biodegradation of corn straw was effectively accomplished in all acid

451    pretreatments. Among the studied acids (CH3COOH, HCl and H2SO4), the corn straw



                                           19

452    pretreated with 2% H2SO4 obtained the highest methane yield of 175.6 mL/g VS ,which was

453   74.6% higher than that of untreated straw. Syaichurrozi et al. (2019) pretreated Salvinia

454   molesta biomass by 4% H2SO4 and generated 81.8% higher biogas production with shortened

455    lag phase. Saha et al. (2018) achieved a 10.0% increase in methane yield after 0.2 M acetic acid

456    pretreatment of mixed fruit waste. However, growth inhibitors could be produced during DA

457    pretreatment, such as furfural and hydroxymethylfurfural (HMF) which hinder the AD

458   (Jönsson & Martín, 2016).

459       In addition to acid and base, oxidants such as hydrogen peroxide (H2O2) has been

460   commonly used in pulping and bleaching industries for lignin removal. H2O2 can break down

461    the structure of lignocellulose through releasing hydroxyl radicals (e.g., HO· and HOO·) and

462   molecular oxygen at low concentration via strong oxidation ability (Mao et al., 2015). Unlike

463    alkaline or DA pretreatment, peroxide pretreatment can be used at relatively mild concentration,

464   temperature and atmospheric pressure, while  effectively removing  lignin from various

465    lignocellulosic agricultural residues (Cabrera et al., 2014). When Miscanthus floridulus was

466    treated by 0.8% H2O2 for 24 h, the methane yield of 279 mL/g VS was achieved, which was

467  49% higher than the control assay (Katukuri et al., 2017). Liu et al. (2018) demonstrated that

468    peroxidation through H2O2 was a useful method to disintegrate sludge, leading to higher sCOD

469   and increased methane production by 19.89% when microwave-H2O2 pretreatment applied.

470       Biological pretreatment is considered as environmental-friendly and inexpensive technique

471    for AD as this process does not require high energy and chemical inputs for operation (Zhao et

472     al., 2018). Previous researches have tried to improve the AD process by using anaerobic or

473    aerobic predigestion or enzyme addition (Atelge et al., 2020). The anaerobic pretreatment

474    predigests the substrate under mesophilic or thermophilic environments (Neumann et al., 2016).

475   For anaerobic pretreatment of sewage sludge, temperature phased anaerobic digestion (TPAD)

476     is a commonly applied choice for which a primary or hyper thermophilic digester is applied



                                           20

477   with a secondary mesophilic digester (known as two-stage AD) (Ariunbaatar et al., 2014). A

478    recent study performed TPAD on wastewater sludge digestion found a methane release rate of

479   3.55 L CH4 /L day at 45°C along with a 77% reduction in VS (Hameed et al., 2019). For fungal

480    pretreatment, several classes including brown-rot, white-rot, soft-rot and basidiomycete fungi,

481   have been used in pretreatment to increase feedstock solubilization (Shirkavand et al., 2017).

482   Enzymes such as peroxidase and laccase excreted by fungi can directly degrade the lignin and

483    increase the digestibility of substrate in AD (Zheng et al., 2014). The pretreatment of rice straw

484   by wood-decay fungus Pleurotus ostreatus, Phanerochaete chrysosposrium, and Ganoderma

485   lucidum increased 64%, 122% and 88% of gas production, respectively (Kainthola et al., 2019a;

486   Kainthola et al., 2019b). Trichoderma reesei and Aspergillus are investigated in many studies

487    for its capability to excrete cellulase to degrade the insoluble cellulose that is found in large

488    portions in the sludge, food waste and other lignocellulosic biomass (Gerhardt et al., 2007;

489   Nguyen  et  al., 2021). The effects of lysozyme pretreatments on WAS hydrolysis and

490    degradability was evaluated, and Chen et al. (2018) found that lysozymes can increase the

491  sCOD concentration in the sludge by 2.23 times and 2.15 times higher than protease and α-

492   amylase. The sludge flocculation disintegration was also improved. Comparing with the non-

493    biological pretreatment, biological pretreatment generates no toxic compounds (e.g., phenolic

494   compounds), production of potential useful by-products, milder operation condition and low

495    cost for waste disposal which is more compatible with AD (Wagner et al., 2018; Wu & He,

496   2013).

497      While demonstrated to be effective in biomass fractionation, the increased capital and

498    operational costs of different pretreatment processes have hindered the large-scale application

499    of biorefinery. Most of the pretreated substrates are free from microorganisms and ready to be

500    utilized by pure enzyme or single strain. The pretreatment techniques need to apply with

501    specific targets with the production extremely high value products to achieve a more



                                           21

502   economical operation of AD. Figure 6 illustrates the trades of various parameters applied in

503  AD among increased costs from pretreatment, changed methane yield, and extended time of

504    operation. The overall operational costs of enzymatic pretreatment are lower in the report due

505    to its extremely low energy and chemical consumption in physical and chemical pretreatment

506    processes. However, the significant limitation on the application of the biological pretreatment

507    are of its long reaction time and more sensitive responses to the ambient environment (Sindhu

508    et al., 2016). The requirement of long SRT operation reflected into large land requirement has

509   prevented a wide application of biological pretreatment in urbanized areas, while also increase

510    the difficulty of process control and operation.

512   5. Perspectives

513    AD  has  demonstrated  to be  a  useful  selection  for  the  conversion  of  pretreated

514    lignocellulosic substrate and high strength cellulosic waste. With the advances of new

515    generation genomic tools, the dynamic changes of the microbial ecology have been gradually

516    clarified, which has been demonstrated in the example of cellulosome-induced-cellulolysis in

517    this review. Co-digestion of different feedstock, i.e., FW, AW, and/or cellulosic sludge, with

518    activated sludge have been attracting significant attentions in large-scale practices in recent

519    years. However, recent publications on the optimization of substrate-sludge combinations for

520    specific AD process may not represent the total production rates of various waste sources. More

521   advanced technique and understanding will therefore soon become mandatory for a broad range

522    of AD research, i.e., from process design/operation to genetic modification. By clarifying the

523   dockerin-cohesin systems in AD, more effective hydrolyzing tools may be synthesized from

524   wastewater, which benefits cellulose valorization in multi-substrate treatment.

525       For process upgrade, microaeration offers significant benefits to cellulolysis-methanogens

526    interactions in AD, while innovative gas diffusion process, real-time monitoring principles,



                                           22

527   and control techniques are to be investigated in order to optimize the DOTE in the high solid

528    loading environment. The potential residual oxygen in the solid layers and headspace in large

529    scale operation needs to be carefully designed with minimum energy inputs, gas flow, and fire

530    risks. In addition, pretreatment techniques of lignocellulosic biomass has demonstrated its role

531    before bioconversion. Physical, chemical, and biological processes have claimed their niches

532    in  different  beneficial  areas among conversion  efficiency, product  values, and  costs,

533    respectively. While harsh pretreatment may better facilitate the biomass recalcitrant for

534    bioconversion, the “bacteria-free” nature of pretreated substrate leads to an AD (multi-culture)

535   over saccharification (cellulase)/fermentation (single culture) discussion on how to utilize the

536    easily  degradable  substrates  for most  valuable  products.  Future development  of  the

537   pretreatment/AD processes may consider the joint mechanisms applying the energy and/or

538    recycled bioconversion metabolites  (e.g., waste heat, ammonia, organic acid, and other

539    fermentation products) for the development of integrated processes. Separation techniques for

540    treated solid digestate are as importance as conventionally believed for balancing the product

541    values from AD with various critical SRTs to be investigated.

542

543   6. Conclusions

544       Hydrolysis serves as the rate limiting factor of AD receiving lignocellulosic and cellulosic

545   needs to be accelerated by various approaches toward a sustainable bio-economy. This critical

546   review summarized the key biological factors when applying AD for the valorisation of

547    cellulosic biomass waste, including biodegradabilities of lignocellulose biomass, functional

548   microorganisms of cellulolysis, their functional enzyme category, and cellulosomes. The

549    genetic fingerprint of cellulolysis, engineering application of micro-aeration with its inherent

550    genetics changes and pretreatment methods for lignocellulose biomass are also reviewed.
